slides.title: Sample Space
bullets: Sample space S = set of all possible outcomes
talking_points: Why it matters: defining the universe of outcomes lets us assign probabilities rigorously.
Intuition: think of S as the list of every result you could possibly see when you run the experiment.
Example: for a single six-sided die, the sample space is S = {1,2,3,4,5,6}. This captures all six equally possible faces.

slides.title: Events and Set Operations
bullets: Union A∪B, Intersection A∩B, Complement Aᶜ
talking_points: Why it matters: events are the objects we assign probabilities to, and set operations let us combine them.
Intuition: an event is simply a collection of outcomes you care about, like "even roll".
Example: A = {2,4,6} (even), B = {4,5,6} (greater than 3). Union A∪B = {2,4,5,6}, Intersection A∩B = {4,6}. This matches the worked example in the notes.
Common mistake: forgetting that the union counts outcomes appearing in both sets unless you subtract the intersection.

slides.title: Kolmogorov Axioms

equations.explanation: Probabilities are never negative and the whole sample space has probability one.

equations.latex: P ( A \cup B ) = P ( A ) + P ( B ) \text{ if } A \cap B = \emptyset
equations.explanation: For disjoint events the probability of their union is the sum of their individual probabilities.

talking_points: Why it matters: these axioms are the foundation from which all probability rules are derived.
Intuition: think of probability as a weight assigned to sets of outcomes; the whole space must weigh to one and weights cannot be negative.
Connection: from these axioms we can derive formulas for complements and general unions.

slides.title: Addition Rule and Uniform Example

equations.latex: P ( A \cup B ) = P ( A ) + P ( B ) - P ( A \cap B )
equations.explanation: For any two events we subtract the overlap to avoid double‑counting.

talking_points: Why it matters: most real problems involve events that are not disjoint, so we need the full addition rule.
Intuition: start with the sum of probabilities, then remove the part counted twice.
Example: for a fair die, event "even" has 3 favorable outcomes out of 6, giving P(even)=3/6=1/2. This uses the uniform probability formula.
Common mistake: forgetting to subtract P(A∩B) leads to probabilities larger than 1.

slides.title: Conditional probability and independence

equations.latex: P ( A \mid B ) = \frac { P ( A \cap B ) } { P ( B ) }
equations.explanation: The probability of A given B is the joint probability divided by the probability of B.

equations.latex: P ( A \cap B ) = P ( A \mid B ) P ( B )
equations.explanation: Rearranged form, showing how to compute a joint probability from a conditional.

talking_points: Conditional probability tells us how our belief about A changes once we know B happened.
Independence means learning B does not affect the chance of A, so the joint factorises.
Example: drawing two cards without replacement. P(both aces)=4/52 × 3/51≈0.0045; the second factor is P(second ace|first ace).
A common mistake is to treat dependent events as independent and multiply marginal probabilities.

slides.title: Bayes' theorem

equations.latex: P ( B \mid A ) = \frac { P ( A \mid B ) P ( B ) } { P ( A ) }
equations.explanation: Bayes' theorem expresses the reverse conditional probability in terms of the forward one.

talking_points: Bayes' theorem lets us update our belief about B after observing A.
The prior P(B) reflects the initial chance of B, while the posterior P(B|A) is the updated chance.
Example: disease prevalence 1%, test sensitivity 99%, false positive 5%. Posterior ≈0.17, showing most positives are false.
Beware: forgetting to compute P(A) correctly; usually need the law of total probability.

slides.title: Discrete random variables: expectation & variance

equations.latex: E [ X ] = \sum _ { x } x \, p ( x )
equations.explanation: The mean is the weighted average of all possible values.
Variance measures the average squared deviation from the mean.

talking_points: A discrete random variable maps outcomes to numbers; its pmf gives probabilities for each value.
Expectation is linear, making calculations with sums of variables easy.
Example: fair die. E[X]=3.5, E[X²]=91/6, variance≈2.92.
A subtle point: adding a constant shifts the mean but does not change variance.
